posts.post_subject: Can Xenon Pumped Dye Lasers Make Holograms Of People?
posts.content_md:
Given the assumption that an object can only travel 1/4th to 1/2th the wavelength of light being used, during the total exposure time it takes to make a hologram, I did a few simple calculations.

I thought it would be really neat if a Q-swwitched YAG laser, frequency doubled to 532 nm - could catch a bullet flying out of a gun - in mid-air.

So I wanted to know what the maximum velocity of the bullet would be.

The velocity I came up with, for a distance traveled during this time - 

 between 1/4th - 1/2th the wavelength of light being used - was a velocity between 59.5 mph - 119 mph. That would be 95.76 kph - 191.52 kph for those of you on the metric system.

While that may sound fairly fast, the muzzle velocities of guns are usually much higher. But the muzzle velocity could be lowered with a low grain bullet, making such a hologram possible.

Since I was now thinking in terms of maximum velocity, instead of just the amount of distance traveled during exposure time, I decided to do this same calculation for non Q-switched dye lasers.

These have a pulse time of 500 ns.

For a green dye laser; with an output of 540 nm, the maximum distance an object can travel - given the same assumption that this distance must be limited to 1/4th to 1/2th the wavelength of light being used - is ALSO equivalent to a velocity between 0.27 m/sec - 0.54 m/sec.

This translates to a velocity of 270 millimeters - 540 millimeters per second.

Or between 10.63 inches/sec - 21.26 inches/sec.

*********************************************

CONCLUSION: While it may not be possible to capture a bullet in mid-air with a xenon pumped dye laser, it should be possible to make holograms of PEOPLE, PETS, and in general, LIVING ANIMALS.

You wouldn't be able to capture "action scenes" . . . .

But people are already accustomed to "posing" for conventional photographs. The fact that they would ALSO have to pose for a hologram, should not affect them in the slightest.

*********************************************

The only thing that is lacking in a dye laser is coherence length.

But if I'm not mistaken, Q-switched YAG lasers have a very short coherence length also.

In a frequency doubled YAG laser, this problem is solved by filtering the beam through prisms, while discarding the unwanted frequencies of light. The beam is THEN run through an interferometer, which narrows the bandwidth. The final output is then passed through a green filter, eliminating the last few remaining traces of unwanted light.

At least that is my understanding; while attempting to understand the schematics described in a Russian holography studio, that uses a Q-switched YAG laser at 20 ns.

Of course I could be mistaken in my understanding, and also could be off in my calculations.

What do you guys think?

posts.content_md:
These calculations bring back memories!

When I first started DCG holography, about '86 or so, we used a 25W Argon. I got to wondering if it was possible to make pulse holograms of water splashes, bullets etc a la the Edgerton photos ( [http://web.mit.edu/edgerton/](http://web.mit.edu/edgerton/) ). With this much power I reasoned that if a sufficently fast shutter could be found then a 25W laser should be able to zap a Silver film with a sensitivity of 20 odd microjoules in microseconds. I'd also seen a photo of a hologram by some workers (Ralph Wuerker?, Jim Trollinger?) in TRW purporting to be a hologram of a bullet. Anyway, I calculated the speed of an object at which it might be possible to do this and, to my amazement, found that a bullet was too fast for a pulse hologram (my figures were pretty much the same as yours, if memory serves). The famous photo of the holographic bullet was fake! Some years later I got to know someone working at TRW who knew the author of the bullet hologram and I askied about it. It turned out that the bullet hologram was actually a shadowgram, in which case, it is possible to capture a bullet in flight holographically.

About holograms of live animals. I've never done this, but I believe the limitation is the slight pulsating of skin due to parastolic and systolic blood pressure. So even though the figures appear to be perfectly still, their skins are pulsating down at the micron level.

> About holograms of live animals. I've never done this, but I believe the limitation is the slight pulsating of skin due to parastolic and systolic blood pressure. So even though the figures appear to be perfectly still, their skins are pulsating down at the micron level.

Hans Bjelkhagen and I along with a grad student named Marc Friedman made some SBR holograms of human hand and the inside of the colon of a dog with a CW argon laser. These holograms were tiny, smaller in diameter than a dime. The light was delivered via a fiber optic, as the project revolved around using holographic endoscopes.

The exposure was mechanically timed with a conventional iris shutter in front of the fiber launcher to be used as a "pulse plucker" and a spinning disc with slits whirring in front of the laser to shape the pulse down to the microsecond realm by chopping.

Ilford Green Holo film was used and developed in SM-6. The holograms worked! It is definitely feasible to record holograms of living tissue with CW lasers if the exposures are in the microsecond region.

posts.content_md:
Well, pulling out the famous back-of-an-envelope ...

The average heartbeat of an average person (whoever that is) is about 60 a minute. This is about 1 Hz. I don't know the amplitude but a human hair is about 50 microns, so if we assume 1/10th of a human hair, that gives an amplitude of 5 microns. Thus skin moves at about 20 microns/sec or 40 lambda/sec (remember that peak occurs at 1/4 period). In order to limit motion to less than 1/4 lambda, you'd have exposure times of 6.25 ms. Now assume that you're exposing a 4x5 (10cm x 12.5cm) film with a sensitivity of 150 microjoules/sq cm (typical figures for todays emulsions), you need to zap the plate with 18.75 mJ in 6.25 ms or 3125 W. That's an awful lot of power (but check the calculation, I'm prone to arithmetical errors. Well known fact: mathematicians can't add!) With a pulse, this is pretty easy, but with cw I'm not sure it's that easy unless you do it with a fairly small area, as Ed Wesley and Hans did. So, not impossible, but not easy either.

Eye safety is another issue, since the output of homemade dye lasers might vary, depending on any number of conditions; and even from one pulse to the next. And even then, they should close their eyes - just in case.

I think this should be done even with a divergent beam.

Otherwise, I suspect that the range of laser pulse durations that is possible in holography, is much larger than many people believe. And if this is true, then extending the range of subjects that can be hologramed MIGHT make holography a little more common.

I have been looking into using a pulsed dye laser for holography and I think it can be done. There are some problems; the dye laser light will need to be modified by additional optics to provide better spatial and temporal coherence. You’re dealing with dyes, solvents, high voltage- high current circuits and it’s putting out a lot of light energy, so you need to think about eye protection. Aligning up the optics won’t be an easy task because your working with pulsed light. The biggest safety issue I believe, is the high voltage- high current used for the flash tubes. On the other side of the coin the repetition rate of the flash lamp would be very low, one shot per hologram. Which would simplify construction. The advantages of a pulsed dye laser light be huge, no stability problem, and the ability to tune it to almost any wave length of visible light. There are sites on the net detailing construction of homemade dye lasers but, the construction articles don’t deal with coherence, but with additional optics I think the beam can be cleaned up. posts.post_subject: Can Xenon Pumped Dye Lasers Make Holograms Of People?
posts.content_md:
Over the years, I've had an interest in dye lasers for holography. As Sergio pointed out, they have certainly been used for this purpose.

But a person has to be practical, and the first question should be this: *Which* dye laser do I intend to use? And just as important, *how* will I get it?

I'm of the opinion that dye lasers are the ultimate form of laser, because they can do many things the others simply cannot. And since the lasing medium is a fluid, it can be rapidly pumped out of the excitation zone (as rapidly as necessary). So, they can be scaled up in power to an almost arbitrary limit, since they can dissipate heat like no other type of laser can. And, if I'm not mistaken, dye lasers hold the record for the narrowest linewidth for any type of laser. Add to this the fact that they can produce any color in the visible spectrum.

What is the cost for this kind of performance? I would define it as incredible, in terms of complexity. I would say that buying a dye laser suitable for holography is pretty much out of the question. So we're left with the prospect of building one. Another tremendous task. Of course, you could build the one in Scientific American. Even that is dangerous and quite difficult. But the *power* is they key isssue. It simply doesn't have enough for a pulsed laser for holography. If the ouput had a decent coherence length, perhaps then it could be used. But it doesn't. And if you want sufficient coherence, you will need to narrow the linewidth by using a resonator with a grating (probably one in the grazing incidence configuration, or one in which the beam is expanded first before it reaches the grating). The simple grating setup shown in Scientific American isn't sufficient. This grating will reduce power drastically, and increase the complexity of the laser.

Honestly, I've given the matter a lot of thought, and I did intend to build a *repetitively pulsed* dye laser which I estimated to have a *time averaged* coherence length of approximately 5 centimeters. Even this modest amount of coherence involves an incredible amount of work and substantial expense. I've decided it's not worth it, and have given up.

As we've mentioned here before, there are many, many ways of "theoretically" solving any problem. The "nothing is impossible" crowd can always come up with a way to do anything as a thought expreriment. We've also seen some pretty bizarre ideas being floated. However, it seems that the practical ability to carry out these ideas experimentally is far more of a measure of "can it be done". Usually, my answer is, "do it!" I think that the question of whether it's worth doing at all is a seperate question to "can it be done". If it can be done, and there are advantages to doing it, then maybe technology will find a way to do it on a practical basis. Even if there are no apparent advantages to it being done, one may be found. The history of the laser exactly follows this path from "Can it be done", to "yes, but it's very, very difficult and completely impractical" to "Now we've made it easy and more practical, what do we do with it?" to "How could we have ever lived without it"!

If the only practical problems with Q switched dye lasers are coherence and eye safety, it seems that these are not insurmountable. Spatial coherence doesn't seem to be a problem. For temporal coherence, use a thick, Bragg grating, or even a stack of them. Surely a cw HeNe or something could be used to track the beam through the same optics before firing to avoid accidentally being zapped by a stray beam. Even the 5cm mentiioned by Joe is more than enough to zap an insect, which is a beginning. Start maybe by shooting a worm. They're blind anyway, so eye protection won't be an issue!

posts.content_md:
I don't know if it will help or not, but I have been doing some reading on the net. One of the reasons that helium - neon lasers are so stable in their coherence - is that they have about 3 modes of possible oscillation. The dye laser, by contrast has 5,000 modes, all separated by 19 nm of wavelength.

If power is a problem, then it might be possible to use one dye laser as an oscillator, and another as an amplifier. This is how the Russians have their holographic YAG laser set up. In order for this to work, the Xenon lamps from both lasers have to be perfectly synchronized.

I doubt if power will be the main problem, however, in the initial testing phase. The main thing is to try to get some kind of temporal coherence. Since these dye lasers are tunable, I'm wondering if some kind of phase locked loop - or fringe lock - would be possible. That would be something that could best be tested while running in CW mode. 

Of course, it wouldn't be true CW, because you would still have a series of pulses. 

It might be easier at first, to output the same kind of light that you would normally get from laser diodes. You probably already have the holographic plates and developer for that; so you can use what you already have. And use the smallest and least expensive plates you have, since few people succeed in anything on their first try. 

That's true even when you are doing things that others have done before; let alone trying anything new.

posts.post_subject: Can Xenon Pumped Dye Lasers Make Holograms Of People?
posts.content_md:
Years ago I was quite determined to make a dye laser for holography. There was one paper in particular that caught my attention: "Narrow linewidth operation of a flashlamp-pumped dye laser" by J.H. Zhang, B.R. Hilty, and H.A. Schuessler from Texas A&M University. This was published in Volume 21, Number 17 (September 1982) of Applied Optics, pages 3065-7.

I've read many, many papers (and books) on dye lasers, including some where dye lasers were used for holography. But this is the one I wanted to use as a starting point, because *I think* the laser these authors describe could be used for holography, not as a "single pulse" laser like ruby, but essentially as a CW laser, except that the beam would consist of a series of mutually-coherent pulses at say 50 pulses per second (more or less). I realize this sounds odd (and improbable), but, according to the paper, they achieve a "multipulse" or time-averaged linewidth of 1.3 GHz. By comparison, a HeNe laser has a typical linewidth of 1.4GHz. They also state that the average power of their laser is 140mW, at 50 pulses per second, each pulse lasting 2 microseconds. (The peak power was 1.4 kW.)

I will quote the opening paragraph of the paper:

"Currently a pulsed due laser design using a grazing incidence mounted grating and a tuning mirror (references 1 & 2) or a second Littrow mounted grating (reference 3) is being used extensively for nitrogen laser and Nd:YAG laser pumped dye lasers. The pulse duration and the peak power of these tunable dye lasers are typically in the range of several nanoseconds and kilowatts. Since in some nonlinear spectroscopy experiments there is an important need to obtain more photons per laser pulse than in these lasers, a long pulse duration flashlamp-pumped dye laser at similar power levels is a good candidate to achieve this goal. So far a grazing incidence grating and mirror (reference 4) arrangement was used to tune a coaxial flashlamp-pumped dye laser thereby achieving a time-averaged linewidth of 2.4 GHz. This Letter describes a different laser geometry using both a grazing incidence grating and a Littrow mounted grating as well as an elliptical cavity for efficient flashlamp pumping. The two-grating combination, together with the small beam divergence produced by the dye capillary and several apertures inside the cavity, improves the time-averaged linewidth to 1.3 GHz. For single laser pulses a linewidth of <600 MHz is observed. The laser described operates with a repetition rate of more than 50 Hz without a loss of laser power."

posts.content_md:
A muffler? Good try but for a single lamp cavity the focal points of both sides of the ellipse needs to be at the center of the rod on one end the then center of the lamp on the other. Another thing I have not seen mentions is the power (capacitor) needed to flash these Xenon lamps. Pretty heavy duty and dangerous. Another consideration is how to tune and tweak the oscillator if you are only getting very short pulses at a single pulse per second or less (1Hz). You could speed up the repetition rate for tuning but then you would have to water cool the lamp and rod. Also, you would have to build a stable rail to hold the oscillator, the two mirrors, the KDP if used, the q-switch and any other components needed. Furthermore, anything that is varied like cavity temperature, pulse rate, mirror percentage reflectivity, capacitor parameter results in a different mode. Simply aligning the optics with an external laser may get it lasing but fine tweaking for holography has to be done with the real time beam. I used to build Pulsed Yag Lasers for Lenox Laser and design software to vary the repetition rate from 50pps to 1 pulse per 5 seconds with the option to fire one pulse only. They were water cooled and the power supply, including capacitors, was as big as a refrigerator. They were putting out about 2 to 5 joules each. Single cavity, dual cavity, osc/amp, frequency doubled, intra cavity attenuation (helps a lot to clean the beam) depending on your crystal, different mirror reflectivity percentages, length of oscillator, where cavity is in oscillator, etc... Many, many parameters to deal with.

I am not saying building your own pulsed system is impossible but if you are going to build your own system start with a known designed and matched cavity with crystal and lamp. And make sure your power supply matches your lamp. Make sure the crytal is suitable for holography in itself. Many are not. Then build your laser.

With regards to building a dye laser for holography: If someone could spend eight hours a day working on it, for months on end, perhaps it could be done.

I tend to think in terms of color holography, as such I need three lasers. Years ago, the dye laser idea was attractive because the choice of wavelengths is quite important, and of course dye lasers have total flexibility in the visible region.

But today, the laser problem doesn't appear to be as serious as it was before. For example, powerful surplus HeNe's can be bought for a reasonable price. For example, I just bought a SP-107 (from a fellow in Milwaukee) that is doing 34mW, for just $500. And my SP-127 has finally been repaired (the cost was only $250 for the repair, since it didn't need to be regassed after all). It's also doing 34mW.

And now that the 315M's are available as surplus for $1,000, the green problem is taken care of. So for my 315M-100 (which is doing 126mW) and the SP-107, my total cost was $1,500. For this $1,500, the red and green are taken care of. At least for 8 X 10's on PFG-03C, I think.

Now, as we all know, blue is a problem. The cost for a suitable argon with an etalon is in the $7,000 to $9,000 range. Plus water cooling and three phase power. I have been told by someone experienced in color holography on PFG-03C that much more power is needed in the blue as opposed to green. (It seems that the least amount of power is needed in the red, which is fortunate.)

Actually, I think Danny is on the right track with his Melles Griot laser. Perhaps the best solution to the blue problem is to buy a non-functioning 400mW laser for a fairly low price, then have have Melles Griot fix it. According to his numbers, this seems to be the most cost-effective way to go. I think it's important to remember that 488nm (argon) is*too long a wavelength for color holography.* So something shorter is needed at substantial power. I was wondering, by the way, if the two beams (each 200mW) from the Melles Griot laser are mutually coherent. In other words, do they come from the same cavity (could you use one for the reference beam, and the other for the object)?

It's true that the crystal has to be doped with Neodynium before it can be lased. But, I believe that an Nd:YAG crystal is not as important as the cavity. The doping ratios are important to get inversion population, but unless you dope it yourself, commercially available Nd:YAG crystals will cause population inversion. The key to laser action is in the cavity design. The doping level will determine the amount of stimulated emission and hence the lasing efficency. 

If you do decide to dope your own crytslas, then certainly care has to be taken to get the conditions and geometry right for the purity needed.

ALthough I was trying to go on memory, I decided to do some research to try to back up what I have stated. I forgot to mention the flatness of the ends of the rod and the perpendicularity of the ends. Also, when a rod is made it is made from a "block" of crytal, cutting out the optically best part. Inferior rods may come from the second standard cuts which are typically much less expensive. I don't want to belabor this point, but the crystal is very important for holography.

When single mode (TEM00) operation is required, the selection of proper dopant concentration is critical to the system's operation.

[http://www.photonic.saint-gobain.com/Me ... Nd_YAG.pdf](http://www.photonic.saint-gobain.com/Media/Documents/S0000000000000001020/Nd_YAG.pdf)

*For applications where TEM00 single mode operation is

required, it is necessary to reduce or eliminate the variations in

the bulk material and in the absorption of the pumping radiation

throughout the component. In addition, wavefront distortions due

to geometric imperfections and thermal gradient effects such as

thermal lensing must be minimized.

*Geometric and material imperfections in an Nd:YAG laser

rod cause poor beam quality and sometimes reduce the power

output of a laser gain component. Key indicators of laser gain

component optical quality are wavefront distortion, birefringence

variation, and extinction ratio.

*Wavefront distortion of a laser rod is expressed in terms of

the distortion of a plane wave that is propagated through the rod.

The distortion of the wavefront is a consequence of any variation

in the optical path length through the component, caused by inhomogeneities

and strain in the crystal or geometric imperfections.
